Lake: a continuous effect, raw source data

Source: vignettes/lake.Rmd
lake.Rmd

This follows MixSIAR’s lake example (its lake_ex vignette), whose data are simulated based on Francis et al. (2011, Ecology Letters, doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2011.01597.x): zooplankton in 21 lakes, two tracers (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) and three sources (terrestrial detritus, surface particulate organic matter (POM) and subsurface POM). The diet changes along a continuous effect, each lake’s ratio of Secchi depth to mixing depth (Secchi.Mixed), a measure of how far light reaches into the mixed layer. The source data are raw samples, and the error structure is Residual only. Only the fitting call differs from MixSIAR’s: run_pfn() in place of write_JAGS_model() and run_model().

The data 

mix <- load_mix_data(
  filename = system.file("extdata", "lake_consumer.csv", package = "MixSIARPFN"),
  iso_names = c("d13C", "d15N"), factors = NULL, fac_random = NULL,
  fac_nested = NULL, cont_effects = "Secchi.Mixed")
source <- load_source_data(
  filename = system.file("extdata", "lake_sources.csv", package = "MixSIARPFN"),
  source_factors = NULL, conc_dep = FALSE, data_type = "raw", mix)
#> Raw source data summarised to means, SDs and sample sizes (Subsurface POM: n = 21; Surface POM: n = 21; Terrestrial Detritus: n = 21).
discr <- load_discr_data(
  filename = system.file("extdata", "lake_discrimination.csv", package = "MixSIARPFN"),
  mix)

load_source_data() summarises the raw source samples to each source’s mean, SD and sample size, which is what MixSIARPFN’s networks use:

source$data
#>                 Source  Meand13C   SDd13C   Meand15N   SDd15N  n
#> 1       Subsurface POM -34.10900 1.145290  0.5945238 2.981343 21
#> 2          Surface POM -29.13057 1.277247  0.3585714 2.090102 21
#> 3 Terrestrial Detritus -29.51352 1.020728 -3.0205238 1.373461 21

There are 21 lakes (one consumer row each), with Secchi.Mixed from 0.09 to 7.23.

plot_data(mix = mix, source = source, discr = discr)

Fitting the model

Residual only error and MixSIAR’s uninformative Dirichlet prior, as in MixSIAR’s vignette.

time <- system.time(
  fit <- run_pfn(mix, source, discr, alpha.prior = 1,
                 resid_err = TRUE, process_err = FALSE)
)
fit
#> MixSIARPFN fit (Residual only error), 3 sources, in 0.3 s
#> Marginal posteriors (no joint draws). Global diet:
#>                source  mean    sd  2.5% 97.5%
#>        Subsurface POM 0.449 0.211 0.045 0.843
#>           Surface POM 0.465 0.206 0.055 0.849
#>  Terrestrial Detritus 0.158 0.146 0.003 0.537
#> Use output_pfn() for every proportion and parameter.

Results 

out <- output_pfn(fit, mix, source,
                  output_options = list(summary_save = FALSE, plot_post_save_pdf = FALSE))

The diet along Secchi.Mixed, as in MixSIAR’s vignette:

for (p in out$plots[grepl("Secchi", names(out$plots))]) print(p)

From the lowest to the highest Secchi.Mixed, the share of Subsurface POM rises from 0.15 to 0.97 and the share of Surface POM falls from 0.74 to 0.02.

Comparison with MixSIAR 

ref <- mixsiar_reference("lake")
ref_raw <- mixsiar_reference("lake_raw")
blocks <- character(0)

With a continuous effect, each consumer has its own diet. Each lake’s diet from MixSIARPFN against MixSIAR’s (MixSIAR’s p.ind), along Secchi.Mixed:

plot_compare_covariate(fit, ref$pind)

The two curves follow each other closely: the consumers’ posterior mean diets differ by 0.044 on average.

The global diet (at the average Secchi.Mixed) and the residual multipliers:

MixSIAR 3.1.12 fitted the same model to the same data with 3 chains of 300,000 iterations (burn-in 200,000, MixSIAR’s “long” run), which took 6 minutes (largest Gelman-Rubin diagnostic 1.048). MixSIARPFN took 0.3 seconds, about 1,100 times faster.

Means, SDs, 95% intervals and the Wasserstein-1 distance between the two posteriors (W1: how far, on average, one posterior’s mass has to move to match the other, on the proportion scale):

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  quantity = cmp$name,
  `MixSIARPFN mean` = round(cmp$pfn_mean, 3), `MixSIAR mean` = round(cmp$mixsiar_mean, 3),
  `MixSIARPFN SD` = round(cmp$pfn_sd, 3), `MixSIAR SD` = round(cmp$mixsiar_sd, 3),
  `MixSIARPFN 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", cmp$pfn_q2.5, cmp$pfn_q97.5),
  `MixSIAR 95% CI` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", cmp$mixsiar_q2.5, cmp$mixsiar_q97.5),
  W1 = round(cmp$w1, 3), check.names = FALSE))
quantity MixSIARPFN mean MixSIAR mean MixSIARPFN SD MixSIAR SD MixSIARPFN 95% CI MixSIAR 95% CI W1
p.global.Subsurface POM 0.449 0.480 0.211 0.221 0.04 to 0.84 0.04 to 0.81 0.046
p.global.Surface POM 0.465 0.363 0.206 0.187 0.05 to 0.85 0.04 to 0.83 0.101
p.global.Terrestrial Detritus 0.158 0.157 0.146 0.195 0.00 to 0.54 0.00 to 0.71 0.042 
for (b in blocks) print(plot_compare(fit, ref$draws, block = b))
plot_compare(fit, ref$draws, type = "means")

What this shows. MixSIARPFN’s diet proportions differ from MixSIAR’s by 0.045 on average (MixSIAR’s posterior SDs are about 0.20), the mean W1 between the two posteriors is 0.063, and the median ratio of their SDs is 0.95. The largest difference in a posterior mean is for p.global.Surface POM (0.465 against 0.363).

The source data here are raw samples, which MixSIARPFN summarises to each source’s mean, SD and sample size. MixSIAR’s own example fits the raw samples instead, estimating each source’s mean and variance in the model. That MixSIAR fit (16 minutes, largest Gelman-Rubin diagnostic 1.135, so not fully converged) and MixSIAR’s fit to the summaries differ by 0.024 in posterior means on average. The comparison above is like for like: both methods fitted the same summaries.
